title: The Impact of Urodynamic Findings on Fatigue and Depression in People with Multiple Sclerosis
condition_or_topic: Relationships between urodynamic findings, fatigue, and depression in people with multiple sclerosis (MS).
clinical_background: Fatigue affects up to over 90% of people with MS and can substantially impair quality of life and earning capacity; depression affects almost one in two. Neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD) may develop in up to 80% of people with MS. Earlier studies reported associations between lower urinary tract symptoms and fatigue or depression, but relied on reported symptoms, which do not reliably identify the underlying type of NLUTD. The relationship between objectively assessed NLUTD and fatigue had not previously been investigated.
objectives: Examine the relationships between urodynamic study findings and fatigue and depression in people with MS to better understand how these symptoms interact.
clinical_question: In people with MS, are findings indicative of NLUTD on urodynamic studies, compared with findings not indicative of NLUTD, associated with fatigue or depression as assessed by FSMC and ADS?
study_design: Retrospective observational analysis of urological, fatigue, and depression data collected prospectively between February 2017 and September 2021.

population.description: People with multiple sclerosis receiving inpatient neurological rehabilitation. Inclusion did not depend on disease course or severity.
inclusion_criteria: Definitive multiple sclerosis diagnosis according to the McDonald criteria.
exclusion_criteria: Being under the age of majority.
Untreated acute lower urinary tract infection.
Refusal to provide written informed consent.
population.care_setting: Neuro-urological department of an inpatient neurological rehabilitation centre.

comparators: People with versus without UDS findings indicative of NLUTD.

People with versus without each individual UDS finding indicative of NLUTD: first desire to void < 100 mL, strong desire to void < 250 mL, abnormal sensation, maximum cystometric bladder capacity < 250 mL, bladder compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O, DO, or DSD.
Normal, increased, and reduced bladder sensation.

primary: Fatigue severity measured by the Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions (FSMC) total score and motor and cognitive subscales; clinically relevant fatigue was defined by a total score of ≥43 or a motor or cognitive subscale score of ≥22.

Depressive symptoms measured by the Allgemeine Depressionsskala (ADS), the German version of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D); a score of >22 indicated clinically relevant depression in the normal German population.

statistical_methods: The cohort and UDS findings were described. Logistic regression models assessed clinically relevant fatigue and depression, with relative risks determined for people with versus without abnormal UDS findings. T-tests compared mean continuous FSMC and ADS scores between groups, and linear models adjusted for gender and age were used. Logistic models examined sensation categories; a likelihood ratio test determined whether sensation had significant explanatory power before individual categories were compared. Analyses used R, with p-values < 0.05 considered statistically significant.
interpretation: In this retrospective cohort of people with MS, UDS findings indicative of NLUTD as a whole were associated with a higher observed risk of clinically relevant fatigue, but the association was not statistically confirmed. Individual findings related to impaired bladder storage were associated with fatigue: reduced compliance and FDV < 100 mL with higher motor-fatigue scores, and reduced compliance, MCBC < 250 mL, and hypersensitivity with greater risk of clinically relevant fatigue. No effect on depression was identified. The study design does not establish causality.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier studies linked patient-reported LUTS to fatigue and depression, whereas a study using bladder diaries found associations with depression for nocturia and urgency but not for voided volume or incontinence. The present fatigue findings resemble earlier bladder-diary findings in which urgency and reduced voided volume had the most correlations with fatigue. A previous study of sexual dysfunction in people with MS likewise found no difference in depression according to the presence of DO. The authors note that prior work had not systematically examined fatigue in relation to objective UDS findings.
clinical_implications: Bladder-storage abnormalities may be relevant to fatigue in people with MS, although the direction and cause of the relationship remain uncertain.

The absence of an observed depression association with UDS findings, despite previously reported links between depression and LUTS, suggests that depression may influence how LUTS are perceived and rated; the authors consider a shared underlying physical cause less likely, without ruling it out.
Understanding relationships among NLUTD, fatigue, and other MS symptoms may help identify therapeutic synergies that improve quality of life.
limitations: Nearly 95% of the cohort had fatigue, leaving few participants without fatigue for statistical comparison.
All participants were receiving inpatient neurological rehabilitation, creating selection bias and potentially favouring inclusion of more severe MS cases.

Detrusor hypocontractility/underactivity was excluded from the analysed definition of NLUTD because it could not be established from a urodynamic measurement alone and required additional clinical information.
The study did not examine whether the effects of NLUTD on fatigue and depression differed by gender.
Fatigue measures rely on subjective self-report; the authors also note that questionnaires may overestimate fatigue and capture aspects of secondary fatigue.
The study design cannot determine causal relationships.
The authors note that the FSMC tends to capture persistent fatigue characteristics, whereas the ADS functions more as a screening measure of recent depressive symptoms.
strengths: The authors describe this as the first systematic investigation of fatigue and depression in relation to UDS findings indicative of NLUTD in people with MS.
The analysis used urodynamic findings rather than relying solely on patient-reported urinary symptoms.
open_questions: Why reduced bladder compliance showed the strongest relationship with fatigue among the examined UDS parameters remains unclear.
The direction and causality of relationships among NLUTD, fatigue, and depression remain unresolved.
It is unknown whether successfully treating NLUTD changes fatigue.
The contribution of MS characteristics to fatigue and NLUTD severity remains uncertain in the literature.
future_directions: Conduct prospective longitudinal studies measuring fatigue and depression in the same individuals before and after NLUTD treatment.
Include urodynamic findings alongside questionnaires and bladder diaries when studying the effects of NLUTD treatment.
Study outpatients with MS, in whom the authors expect a lower proportion with fatigue, and consider alternative fatigue or depression assessment tools.
Undertake a separate, extensive analysis of gender-specific differences.
Investigate how neural damage shown by imaging relates to urological and neuropsychiatric symptoms to clarify their multidirectional relationships and potentially identify therapeutic approaches.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Fatigue and depression are frequent in multiple sclerosis (MS) and substantially diminish quality of life. Associations between symptoms of neurogenic lower urinary tract dysfunction (NLUTD), fatigue, and depression were already described, but the influence of pathological urodynamic study (UDS) findings had not been examined. This retrospective observational study related prospectively collected UDS findings from 274 people with MS (PwMS), obtained between February 2017 and September 2021, to scores on the Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions and the German version of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale. Abnormal findings comprised first desire to void (FDV) < 100 mL, strong desire to void (SDV) < 250 mL, abnormal sensation, detrusor overactivity, detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia, maximum cystometric bladder capacity (MCBC) < 250 mL, and compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O. Motor fatigue scores were significantly higher with compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O (mean difference 3.21, 95% CI 0.25; 6.17, p = 0.036) or FDV < 100 mL (mean difference 2.61, 95% CI 0.1; 5.12, p = 0.041). Clinically relevant fatigue was more likely with MCBC < 250 mL (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 1.02; 1.1, p = 0.006) or compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O (relative risk 1.06, 95% CI 1.02; 1.1, p = 0.004). No effect on depression was identified. The authors call for prospective longitudinal assessment of whether successful NLUTD treatment affects fatigue and permits therapeutic synergies that improve quality of life.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Fatigue is among the most frequent and burdensome MS symptoms; reported prevalence reaches up to over 90% in PwMS. It is difficult to treat and adversely affects health-related quality of life and earning capacity. Physical fatigue involves muscle weakness and consequent exhaustion. Cognitive fatigue may precede MS diagnosis and involves diminished cognitive performance associated with concentration difficulties, memory problems, or emotional instability. Depression affects almost one in two PwMS. MS-related inflammation, demyelination, axonal injury, and brain atrophy are proposed common causes; sleep disturbance, medication adverse effects, and physical or psychological strain from neurogenic bowel or lower urinary tract symptoms are described as secondary causes. NLUTD can occur at initial diagnosis or develop as MS progresses in up to 80% of PwMS. Central nervous system lesion location and severity can disrupt bladder storage and voiding. Detrusor overactivity (DO) occurs at a frequency of 43–62%, detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia (DSD) in 25–35% of cases, and detrusor underactivity (DU) or acontractility in around 20%. Resulting lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS), alongside musculoskeletal, visual, concentration, bowel, and sexual difficulties, contribute to substantial physical and psychosocial strain and significantly reduced quality of life. Earlier studies associated neurogenic LUTS with fatigue and reported significant relationships between LUTS and depression in PwMS. They documented LUTS through histories, questionnaires, or bladder diaries, which can be influenced by personal circumstances and perceived distress. Reported LUTS cannot reliably identify the objective underlying NLUTD type. Because objective NLUTD had not been studied in relation to fatigue, the authors sought to examine how urodynamic findings relate to fatigue and depression.

document_sections.heading: 2. Patients and Methods
document_sections.content: The investigators retrospectively analysed prospectively collected neuro-urological and cognitive-rehabilitation data. They assessed both overall UDS findings indicative of NLUTD and individual abnormal urodynamic parameters in relation to clinically relevant fatigue or depression and to continuous fatigue and depression scores.

document_sections.heading: 2.1. Patients
document_sections.content: The study included 274 PwMS treated in the neuro-urology department of an inpatient neurological rehabilitation centre between February 2017 and September 2021. The Department of Neuro-Urology collected urological data prospectively; the Department of Cognitive Rehabilitation supplied fatigue and depression data. Eligibility required age of at least 18 years, a definitive MS diagnosis according to the McDonald criteria, ability to answer questions, and written informed consent. Disease course and severity did not determine eligibility. Exclusions comprised minors, pregnant or breastfeeding women, people with untreated acute lower urinary tract infections, and those declining written consent. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki, obtained written consent, and received ethical approval (EK 313/13-University Hospital Bonn).

document_sections.heading: 2.2. Fatigue Assessment
document_sections.content: The Fatigue Scale for Motor and Cognitive Functions (FSMC) measured fatigue presence and severity. It has 20 items, with 10 for motor fatigue and 10 for cognitive fatigue; responses range from never (1) to almost always (5). Clinically relevant fatigue was defined by a total score of ≥43 or a motor or cognitive subscale score of ≥22.

document_sections.heading: 2.3. Depression Assessment
document_sections.content: Depressive symptoms were assessed with Allgemeine Depressionsskala (ADS), the German version of the Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D). Its 20 self-report items address the previous 2 weeks and use responses from rarely (0) to mostly (3). A total score of >22 indicates clinically relevant depression in the normal German population. The emphasis on cognitive rather than somatic or fatigue-related items was intended to reduce measurement overlap between depression and fatigue.

document_sections.heading: 2.4. Urodynamic Studies
document_sections.content: A small, experienced neuro-urology team conducted UDS with an MMS Nexam Pro Urodynamic System, following ICS and International Continence Society standards and a consistent clinical procedure. Findings considered indicative of NLUTD were FDV < 100 mL, SDV < 250 mL, any abnormal sensation, MCBC < 250 mL, bladder compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O, and any DO or DSD. Detrusor hypocontractility/underactivity was excluded from this definition because one urodynamic measurement alone cannot establish it. The investigators described the cohort and UDS findings, then examined the overall abnormal-UDS classification and each component separately against binary clinically relevant FSMC and ADS outcomes and continuous FSMC total, motor, cognitive, and ADS scores.

document_sections.heading: 2.5. Statistical Analysis
document_sections.content: Logistic regression models assessed clinically relevant fatigue and depression in relation to abnormal UDS, with relative risks determined for people with versus without abnormal findings. Group means for continuous FSMC and ADS scores were compared with t-tests and linear models adjusted for gender and age. Logistic models evaluated the effects of normal, increased, and reduced sensation on clinically relevant outcomes. A likelihood ratio test first assessed whether sensation quality significantly explained fatigue or depression; individual qualities were compared only when that test was significant. Analyses used R, and p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

document_sections.heading: 3. Results 3.1. Patients and Their Disease Characteristics
document_sections.content: The cohort included 66.8% (183/274) female and 33.2% (91/274) male patients. Mean Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score was 4.25 (SD 1.59; min 1, max 8), with EDSS unavailable for 19.3% (53/274). Mean age was 48.31 years (SD 10.36; min 18, max 73). Mean disease duration at data collection was 10.82 years (SD 8.92; min 0, max 47); duration was unreported by 2.6% (7/274). MS course was primary progressive in 10.2% (28/274), relapsing–remitting in 55.8% (153/274), and secondary progressive in 31.4% (86/274), while 2.6% (7/274) did not specify a course. UDS data were not provided for 9.1% (25/274). Table 1 describes measured urodynamic variables, DO and DSD, and their available and missing observations. Under the prespecified definition, 84.8% (207/244) had UDS findings indicative of NLUTD and 15.2% (37/244) did not. Individual findings were FDV < 100 mL in 23.8% (58/244), SDV < 250 mL in 34.8% (78/224), MCBC < 250 mL in 13.3% (33/249), compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O in 5.0% (12/240), DSD in 36% (81/225), and DO in 32.8% (82/250). Abnormal sensation occurred in 72.0% (180/250): hyposensitivity in 24.0% 60/250, hypersensitivity in 47.2% 118/250, and absent sensation in 0.8% 2/250. Normal sensation occurred in 28.0% (70/250); sensation data were missing for 8.8% (24/274). A high proportion met FSMC criteria for clinically significant fatigue, and approximately half had clinically relevant depression. Table 2 presents the fatigue and depression score distributions, missing data, and proportions above the clinical thresholds. Figure 1 depicts how individual abnormal UDS parameters were distributed among participants with and without fatigue or depression.

document_sections.heading: 3.2. Effects of UDS Findings on Fatigue and Depression
document_sections.content: For the overall category of UDS findings indicative of NLUTD, risks of clinically significant fatigue were higher across the FSMC total and both subscales, but these increases were not statistically confirmed. No corresponding effect was found for clinically significant depression. Mean continuous FSMC total, cognitive, motor, and ADS scores did not differ significantly between participants with and without findings indicative of NLUTD. Thus, the cohort did not demonstrate higher overall fatigue or depression scores in those classified as having abnormal UDS. Table 3 details the binary and continuous comparisons.

document_sections.heading: 3.3. Effects of the Individual UDS Parameters Indicative of NLUTD on FSMC and ADS
document_sections.content: Participants with compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O had significantly higher FSMC motor means than those with higher compliance: mean difference 3.21, 95% CI 0.25; 6.17, p = 0.036. Participants with FDV < 100 mL likewise had higher FSMC motor means than those with FDV ≥ 100mL: mean difference 2.61, 95% CI 0.1; 5.12, p = 0.041. Table 4 presents, for every individual UDS parameter, scores with and without the finding and comparisons for continuous FSMC total, cognitive, motor, and ADS outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 3.4. Effects of Individual Urodynamic Parameters Indicative of NLUTD on Fatigue and Depression
document_sections.content: MCBC < 250 mL and compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O were associated with increased relative risks of clinically relevant fatigue for the FSMC total score and motor subscale. For the total score, the reported relative risks were 1.06 (95% CI 1.02; 1.1, p = 0.006) with MCBC < 250 mL and 1.06 (95% CI 1.02; 1.1, p = 0.004) with compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O. Reduced compliance was also associated with increased risk on the cognitive subscale. Increased relative risk was not shown for the other individual UDS parameters, and no effect on depression was shown. Table 5 provides the fatigue relative risks and adjusted risks by parameter and FSMC outcome. The two asensory PwMS lacked fatigue and depression data and were excluded from the sensation-quality analysis. Pairwise comparisons among normal, hypo-, and hypersensitive participants identified significant differences in clinically relevant fatigue risk across all FSMC categories, but not in depression risk. Except for FSMC mot, normal sensation generally corresponded to the lowest fatigue risk; increased sensation corresponded to the highest. Figure 2 depicts these risks, and Appendix A supplies the detailed comparisons.

document_sections.heading: 4. Discussion
document_sections.content: Previous research linked patient-reported neurogenic bowel and urinary dysfunction with neuropsychological symptoms. The authors state that UDS findings and fatigue had not previously been examined together; a study of MS-related sexual dysfunction had reported depression in relation to urodynamic DO as a secondary finding. In the present cohort of 274 PwMS, UDS findings served as influencing variables and fatigue and depression as outcomes. Overall findings indicative of NLUTD corresponded to higher clinically relevant fatigue risk without statistical confirmation; neither continuous nor binary ADS outcomes showed an effect. Earlier questionnaire studies reported significant associations between LUTS and depression, whereas a bladder-diary study found statistically significant depression associations only for nocturia and urgency, not voided volume or incontinence. The authors note that nocturia may reflect sleep disturbance associated with depression and that urgency is the most subjective diary measure. The earlier sexual-dysfunction study, like the present study, found no depression difference according to DO status. The authors nevertheless suggest that urgency and frequent toileting may contribute to depression. They cite reports of bidirectional LUTS–depression relationships outside MS, improvement in depression after LUTS treatment, adverse effects of low physical activity on depression, and restricted mobility associated with LUTS in PwMS. Their interpretation is that depression may influence perceived LUTS severity more than a shared physical cause explains both conditions; they say direction and causality require further study. They propose that the nonsignificant overall fatigue finding may reflect the large proportion with NLUTD findings and the fact that almost 95% of their cohort had fatigue, leaving small comparison groups. They also caution that fatigue is not clearly defined and that questionnaires may substantially overestimate it and capture secondary-fatigue components, although other studies likewise report high fatigue prevalence. They propose studying MS outpatients, who are expected to have less fatigue, and following individuals' fatigue scores with and without NLUTD treatment. Different fatigue or depression instruments might also be useful: they characterize FSMC as tending to measure enduring everyday fatigue, whereas they describe ADS here as a screening measure of depressive symptoms from the last week. This description of the ADS recall period differs from the previous 2 weeks specified in the methods. In their cohort, reduced bladder compliance and early first desire to void were associated with higher fatigue scores; reduced compliance, reduced MCBC, and hypersensitivity were associated with greater clinically relevant fatigue risk. These findings concern impaired bladder storage. A cited bladder-diary study similarly found the most fatigue associations for urgency and reduced voided volume, and other authors reported adverse psychosocial and cognitive effects of urgency. Carotenuto et al. associated impairment on the Symbol Digit Modality Test (SDMT) with the Neurogenic Bowel Dysfunction Score and the Actionable Bladder Symptom Screening Tool; those authors used that association to justify investigating bladder and bowel function when SDMT is abnormal. Compliance <20 mL/cm H2O was the UDS parameter most closely correlated with fatigue here, but the explanation remains unclear. Research connecting UDS with psychosocial and cognitive disorders is scarce, and the authors report no previous results on correlations among individual urodynamic parameters. Unlike DO or DSD, reduced compliance may represent substantial loss of bladder elasticity resulting from different storage and emptying disorders, so multiple influences are possible. Published findings about fatigue versus MS duration or course conflict, and findings about MS characteristics versus NLUTD severity are inconsistent. This cohort showed no correlation of reduced compliance with patient-specific or MS-specific characteristics. The authors describe this as the first systematic examination of UDS-defined NLUTD findings in relation to both fatigue and depression in PwMS. They identified some fatigue correlations but none for depression; the study design cannot establish causality.

document_sections.heading: 5. Limitations
document_sections.content: The principal limitation was fatigue in nearly 95% of participants, leaving few without fatigue for comparison and restricting correlation analyses. Because every participant was receiving inpatient neurological rehabilitation, selection bias may have favored more severe MS cases requiring rehabilitation. The authors therefore favor longitudinal comparisons within individuals receiving NLUTD treatment. Detrusor hypocontractility/underactivity was omitted from the abnormal-UDS definition because it remains difficult to define through UDS; the examining physician's assessment also draws on bladder diaries and uroflowmetry, so this parameter was not analysed further. The study did not examine whether gender modifies NLUTD effects on fatigue or depression; that question would require a separate extensive analysis. Finally, fatigue instruments rely on subjective patient reports, limiting its measurement and evaluation.

document_sections.heading: 6. Conclusions and Further Directions
document_sections.content: The authors conclude that fatigue correlated significantly with low compliance, reduced cystometric bladder capacity, and hypersensitivity, whereas UDS findings indicative of NLUTD showed no effect on depression despite previously described associations between the symptoms. They call for more detailed investigation of how MS symptoms interact and which direction their relationships take, given the importance of quality of life and therapeutic synergies. They propose prospective longitudinal studies of whether successfully treated NLUTD changes fatigue and other burdensome symptoms. On the basis of their findings, they say NLUTD assessment in such research should include urodynamic findings alongside questionnaires and bladder diaries. They also call for relating neural damage seen with neural imaging modalities to urological and neuropsychiatric symptoms to clarify causality and potentially identify more specific therapeutic approaches.

document_sections.heading: Appendix A
document_sections.content: Table A1 provides likelihood ratio tests, observed and adjusted risks, and pairwise risk ratios for clinically significant FSMC total, cognitive, and motor fatigue and ADS depression across normal, hypersensitive, and hyposensitive sensation. The likelihood ratio tests were significant for FSMC total (LR = 7.8 df = 2 p = 0.021), cognitive (LR = 6.2 df = 2 p = 0.045), and motor fatigue (LR = 6.6 df = 2 p = 0.038), but not for ADS depression (LR = 1.9 df = 2 p = 0.381).

subgroup_analyses: For FDV < 100 mL, clinically relevant fatigue showed no statistically significant association: FSMCsum score ≥ 43, relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.96; 1.09), p = 0.522; FSMCcog ≥ 22, 1.05 (0.93; 1.17), p = 0.456; FSMCmot ≥ 22, 1.01 (0.95; 1.08), p = 0.69. Each comparison is with versus without FDV < 100 mL.

For SDV < 250 mL, clinically relevant fatigue showed no statistically significant association: FSMCsum score ≥ 43, relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.96; 1.09), p = 0.509; FSMCcog ≥ 22, 1.08 (0.97; 1.2), p = 0.173; FSMCmot ≥ 22, 1.01 (0.95; 1.08), p = 0.707. Each comparison is with versus without SDV < 250 mL.

For abnormal sensation, the binary comparison showed no statistically significant association with clinically relevant fatigue: FSMCsum score ≥ 43, relative risk 1.06 (95% CI 0.97; 1.17), p = 0.187; FSMCcog ≥ 22, 1.13 (0.98; 1.31), p = 0.088; FSMCmot ≥ 22, 1.04 (0.96; 1.13), p = 0.353. Each comparison is with versus without abnormal sensation.

For DO, clinically relevant fatigue showed no statistically significant association: FSMCsum score ≥ 43, relative risk 1.00 (95% CI 0.93; 1.08), p = 0.99; FSMCcog ≥ 22, 0.99 (0.88; 1.12), p = 0.9; FSMCmot ≥ 22, 0.99 (0.92; 1.07), p = 0.83. Each comparison is with versus without DO.

For DSD, clinically relevant fatigue showed no statistically significant association: FSMCsum score ≥ 43, relative risk 1.01 (95% CI 0.94; 1.09), p = 0.788; FSMCcog ≥ 22, 0.93 (0.81; 1.07), p = 0.322; FSMCmot ≥ 22, 1.00 (0.93; 1.07), p = 0.993. Each comparison is with versus without DSD.

The analysis of normal, hypersensitive and hyposensitive bladder sensation excluded the two asensory participants because fatigue and depression data were unavailable for them. The likelihood ratio test indicated differences across sensation categories for clinically relevant FSMCsum score (LR = 7.8, df = 2, p = 0.021), FSMCcog (LR = 6.2, df = 2, p = 0.045) and FSMCmot (LR = 6.6, df = 2, p = 0.038), but not ADS (LR = 1.9, df = 2, p = 0.381). The authors reported the greatest fatigue risk with increased sensation and, except for FSMCmot, the lowest with normal sensation. The appendix's cross-comparison matrix does not explicitly establish the direction represented by every risk ratio, so those ratios are not assigned directional interpretations here.

Among participants with normal sensation, the observed risk and adjusted risk, respectively, were 90.38% (95% CI 78.97; 96.8) and 90.83% (82.91; 98.75) for FSMCsum score; 80.77% (67.47; 90.37) and 80.44% (69.58; 91.30) for FSMCcog; 92.31% (81.46; 97.86) and 92.93% (85.90; 99.97) for FSMCmot; and 50.98% (36.6; 65.25) and 49.63% (36.15; 63.11) for ADS.

Among participants with hypersensitive sensation, the observed risk and adjusted risk, respectively, were 98.94% (95% CI 94.21; 99.97) and 99.02% (97.06; 100.00) for FSMCsum score; 94.57% (87.77; 98.21) and 94.11% (88.99; 99.24) for FSMCcog; 98.91% (94.09; 99.97) and 99.01% (97.03; 100.00) for FSMCmot; and 48.91% (38.34; 59.56) and 44.63% (34.25; 55.00) for ADS.

Among participants with hyposensitive sensation, the observed risk and adjusted risk, respectively, were 91.11% (95% CI 78.78; 97.52) and 90.96% (82.29; 99.62) for FSMCsum score; 86.36% (72.65; 94.83) and 85.43% (74.61; 96.26) for FSMCcog; 90.91% (78.33; 97.47) and 90.66% (81.63; 99.69) for FSMCmot; and 38.64% (24.36; 54.5) and 35.98% (22.14; 49.83) for ADS.
secondary_results: The cohort comprised 274 participants: 66.8% (183/274) female and 33.2% (91/274) male. Mean age was 48.31 years (SD 10.36; min 18, max 73); mean EDSS was 4.25 (SD 1.59; min 1, max 8), with EDSS unavailable for 19.3% (53/274). Mean disease duration was 10.82 years (SD 8.92; min 0, max 47), with duration unreported for 2.6% (7/274). Disease course was primary progressive in 10.2% (28/274), relapsing–remitting in 55.8% (153/274), secondary progressive in 31.4% (86/274), and unspecified in 2.6% (7/274).

UDS data were not provided for 9.1% (25/274). Under the predefined definition, 84.8% (207/244) had UDS findings indicative of NLUTD and 15.2% (37/244) did not. The reported individual findings were FDV < 100 mL in 23.8% (58/244), SDV < 250 mL in 34.8% (78/224), MCBC < 250 mL in 13.3% (33/249), compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O in 5.0% (12/240), DSD in 36% (81/225), and DO in 32.8% (82/250). Abnormal sensation occurred in 72.0% (180/250): hyposensitive in 24.0% (60/250), hypersensitive in 47.2% (118/250), and asensitive in 0.8% (2/250). Normosensitivity occurred in 28.0% (70/250); sensation data were unavailable in 8.8% (24/274).

The descriptive UDS table gives, in the order mean (SD), median (25–75%), min–max, valid values % (N), and missing % (N): FDV [mL], 195.2 (121.5), 169 (104; 263.5), 8; 710, 89.4 (245), 10.6 (29); SDV [mL], 292.7 (115.7), 291.5 (2.5; 5), 47; 588, 81.8 (224), 18.2 (50); Compl [mL/cmH2O], 76.2 (66.7), 61.4 (2.0; 14.5), 4; 453, 86.9 (238), 13.1 (36); MCBC [mL], 401.9 (142.0), 406.5 (311.3; 485), 41; 1000, 90.5 (248), 9.5 (26); Reflex volume [cm H2O], 198.2 (109.5), 200 (109.8; 268.8), 10; 449, 29.9 (82), 70.1 (192); Qmax [mL/s], 13.2 (6.6), 13 (8; 18), 2; 37, 46 (126), 54 (148); MV [mL], 330.4 (159.9), 323 (214; 439.5), 9; 715, 83.6 (229), 16.4 (45). For ADS, missing data were 23.7% (65); mean (SD) was 22.49 (11.44), median (25–75%) was 21 (14; 31), min–max was 1; 54, and clinically significant depression occurred in 47.4 (99) of valid observations. main_conclusion: In this retrospective cohort, reduced bladder compliance, reduced cystometric bladder capacity and hypersensitivity were associated with aspects of fatigue, whereas urodynamic findings indicative of NLUTD showed no identified effect on depression. The authors call for prospective longitudinal studies of whether successful NLUTD treatment affects fatigue, using urodynamic findings alongside questionnaires and bladder diaries.
narrative_summary:
This retrospective observational study examined whether objective urodynamic findings were related to fatigue or depressive symptoms in 274 people with multiple sclerosis receiving inpatient neurological rehabilitation. Urological information collected between February 2017 and September 2021 was analysed alongside FSMC fatigue scores and ADS depression scores. UDS findings indicative of NLUTD were present in 84.8% (207/244) of those with the relevant data.

As a combined category, these UDS findings were not significantly associated with clinically relevant fatigue, continuous FSMC scores or ADS scores. Individual storage-related findings yielded more specific associations. Compared with their respective reference groups, participants with FDV < 100 mL had a higher FSMCmot mean, with a mean difference of 2.61 (0.1; 5.12), p = 0.041; for Compliance < 20 mL/cm H2O, the difference was 3.21 (0.25; 6.17), p = 0.036. MCBC < 250 mL was associated with clinically relevant FSMCsum fatigue, with relative risk 1.06 (1.02; 1.1), p = 0.006; the corresponding result for reduced compliance was 1.06 (1.02; 1.1), p = 0.004. Sensation-quality analyses found differences in fatigue risk, but not depression risk.

Interpretation is limited by fatigue affecting nearly 95% of the cohort, the inpatient rehabilitation setting and the inability of the retrospective design to establish causality. The authors propose prospective longitudinal assessment of fatigue after successful NLUTD treatment, incorporating urodynamics as well as questionnaires and bladder diaries.
